## WhatsApp Chain Misinformation Targets Pneumonia Treatment Amidst COVID-19 Concerns

A viral WhatsApp chain is spreading misinformation regarding pneumonia treatment, falsely claiming that current medical approaches are misguided. While the message's specifics are unclear, the underlying sentiment appears to cast doubt on established medical protocols for treating this respiratory illness. This development is particularly concerning given the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, which often presents with pneumonia-like symptoms.

The emergence of this disinformation campaign highlights a recurring theme throughout the pandemic: the spread of inaccurate medical information through social media platforms. While WhatsApp can be a valuable tool for communication, its end-to-end encryption and rapid sharing capabilities also make it a fertile ground for the proliferation of unfounded claims.

The post's assertion that COVID-19 causing thrombosis somehow negates its ability to also cause pneumonia is particularly misleading. Medical understanding has confirmed that COVID-19 can induce both conditions. Thrombosis, or blood clotting, is a recognized complication of severe COVID-19 infections, potentially leading to serious health issues. However, this does not preclude the virus from also causing pneumonia, an inflammation of the lungs that makes breathing difficult.

In fact, pneumonia is a common manifestation of severe COVID-19. The virus can directly damage the lung tissue, leading to fluid buildup and impaired oxygen exchange. To suggest that the existence of thrombosis as a complication somehow disproves the possibility of pneumonia is a dangerous oversimplification of complex medical realities.

The consequences of believing and acting upon this misinformation can be severe. Delaying or refusing appropriate medical treatment for pneumonia, based on these unfounded claims, could lead to worsened symptoms, serious complications, and even death. It is crucial to rely on credible sources of medical information, such as doctors, public health organizations, and reputable medical websites. Sharing unverified information, especially regarding health-related matters, can have detrimental effects on individuals and the wider community.

Ta razvoj je posebej zaskrbljujoč zaradi trajajočega pandemije COVID-19, ki pogosto predstavlja simptome podobne pneumoniji.

Pojav vire nepravilnih informacij poudarja ponavljajočo se temo skozi pandemijo: razširjanje natančnih zdravstvenih informacij prek družbenih omrežij. Trditev v objavi, da povzročanje tromboze pri COVID-19 nekako izključuje možnost, da lahko virus tudi povzroči pneumonijo, je zelo zavajajoča. Tromboza, ali pa krvni koagulacije, je prepoznana komplikacija težkih okužb s COVID-19, ki lahko povzroči resne zdravstvene težave. Vendar pa to ne izključuje, da virus lahko tudi povzroči pneumonijo, vnetje pljuč, ki otežuje dihanje.

Učinki verovanja in delovanja na osnovi te nepravilne informacije lahko so resnično neprijetni. Poudarjanje ali zavrnitev pravega zdravljenja pneumonije zaradi teh nezaključenih trditev lahko vodi do poslabšanja simptomov, resnih posledic in celo smrti. ## Data Gaps Hinder Assessment of PCR Test Reliance in COVID-19 Monitoring

Experts are raising concerns about the availability of granular data regarding COVID-19 testing methodologies, specifically the proportion of Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) tests conducted. While PCR tests have consistently been recognized as the gold standard for accurate COVID-19 detection, the precise volume of PCR testing in relation to other testing methods remains unclear.

This lack of readily accessible information presents a significant challenge for researchers and public health officials attempting to gain a comprehensive understanding of the epidemiological landscape. PCR tests, due to their high sensitivity and specificity, are considered the most reliable method for identifying active COVID-19 infections. Knowing the percentage of total tests comprised of PCR tests would allow for a more accurate assessment of infection rates and disease prevalence within a population.

The inability to determine the precise number of PCR tests administered hinders the ability to effectively compare testing strategies across different regions and time periods. It also complicates efforts to evaluate the impact of variant strains on testing accuracy and the effectiveness of public health interventions.

Without this crucial data, it becomes difficult to ascertain the true extent of COVID-19 transmission and make informed decisions regarding resource allocation and public health policy. A clearer understanding of the reliance on PCR testing is essential for a more robust and reliable assessment of the ongoing pandemic and its potential future trajectories. Further efforts are needed to ensure that detailed testing data, including the specific types of tests used, are collected and made publicly available. This increased transparency will empower public health professionals and researchers to better monitor and manage the continued challenges posed by COVID-19.

## Graphic Circulating Online Misuses WHO Logo, Fuels Misinformation

A graphic circulating widely online is falsely attributed to the World Health Organization (WHO), raising concerns about the spread of misinformation. While the graphic includes the WHO logo, the organization has confirmed that it is not an official document.

The graphic, the content of which is currently unknown, is likely being shared across various social media platforms and potentially even through messaging apps. The inclusion of the WHO logo adds an air of legitimacy, making it difficult for the average user to distinguish between verified information from the WHO and false or misleading content.

The World Health Organization is a specialized agency of the United Nations responsible for international public health. Its official communications are typically disseminated through its website, social media channels, and official press releases. These sources are meticulously vetted and based on scientific evidence, making them crucial resources during public health crises and for general health information.

The misuse of the WHO logo is a serious issue. It allows malicious actors to exploit the organization's reputation and credibility to disseminate false information. This can have potentially harmful consequences, particularly when dealing with sensitive topics like public health guidelines or disease prevention.

The incident highlights the importance of verifying information before sharing it online. Users should always check the source of information, particularly when it relates to health. Look for official sources, such as the WHO website or the websites of national health agencies. Be wary of information shared without attribution or from unverified accounts.

The WHO, and other credible health organizations, routinely issue warnings about misinformation campaigns and provide resources to help the public identify and avoid falling victim to them. Fact-checking websites also play a crucial role in debunking false claims and identifying misleading graphics. Consumers of information should leverage these resources before sharing any health information they find online. This incident serves as a stark reminder to exercise caution and prioritize credible sources in the digital age.

## Grafiks, kas cirkulē interneta, nepareizi atribuēts Pasaules Veselības organizācijai (PVO), izplatās nepatiesības

Grafiks, kas šobrīd plaši cirkulē interneta tīklā, nepareizi atribuēts Pasaules Veselības organizācijai (PVO), kas izraisa bažas par nepatiesību izplatīšanu. Iekļauts grafikā ir PVO logotips, tomēr organizācija ir apstiprinājusi, ka tas nav oficiāls dokumentācijas fragmenta.

Grafika saturs, kas šobrīd nav zināms, tik ilgstoši varētu būt izplatīts dažādos sociālos tīklus un pat caur ziņojumu aplikācijām. PVO logotipa iekļaušana dod izskatu, ka informācija ir oficiāla, kas grūtina vidējam lietotājam atšķirt starp patiesu informāciju no PVO un nepatiesu vai apmulsinošu saturu.

Pasaules Veselības organizācija ir īpaša ārvalstu organizācija, kas atbild par starptautisko publisko veselību. Tās oficiālas komunikācijas tiek izplatītas ar savu tīmekļa vietni, sociālajiem tīkliem un oficiālajiem spiedienādas. Šīs avotu izvēle ir stingri pārbaudīta un balstīta uz zinātniskiem pierādījumiem, tādēļ tos uzskata par svarīgiem resursiem laikā publiskās veselības križāšanas un vispārējiem veselības informācijas sniegšanai.

PVO logotipa neautorizēta izmantošana ir nopietns jautājums. Tas ļauj kaitīgajiem aktoriem izmantot organizācijas reputāciju un ticamību, lai izplatītu nepatiesu informāciju. Šis var izraisīt potenciāli kaitīgus sekas, īpaši, kad runa ir par jutīgām tēmām, piemēram, publiskās veselības norādījumiem vai slimības profilaksei.

Notikums uzsvēra svarīgumu pirms izplatīšanas pārbaudīt informāciju. Lietotāji visiem laikiem nedrīkst izplatīt informāciju, ja tās avots nav skaidrs, īpaši, ja tā saistīta ar veselību. Lūdzu, meklējiet oficiālus avotus, piemēram, PVO tīmekļa vietni vai valsts veselības iestāžu tīmekļa lapas. Būt uz ciešu uz tām informācijai, kas tiek izplatīta bez atribūcijas vai no neapstiprinātām kontām.

PVO un citas ticamas veselības organizācijas bieži izraisa brīdinājumus par nepatiesību izplatīšanas kampaņām un piedāvā resursus, lai palīdzētu sabiedrībai atpazīt un izvairītos no tām. Faktapstākšanas vietnes arī spēj izkropļot nepatiesus apgalvojumus un atklāt apmulsinošus grafikus. Informācijas patērētājiem būtu jāizmanto šie resursi pirms izplatīšanas jebkādu veselības informāciju, ko viņi atrada tīklā. Šis notikums ir ievērojams brīdinājums par uzmanību un ticamu avotu prioritāšanu digitālajā laikmetā.

## Peruvian Health Ministry and WHO Deny Recommending Ginger Chewing as a COVID-19 Remedy

**Lima, Peru** - The Peruvian Ministry of Health (MINSA) and the World Health Organization (WHO) have both issued statements denying the authenticity of a document circulating online that purportedly recommends chewing ginger as a preventative measure or treatment for COVID-19. The denial comes amid a surge in misinformation surrounding the pandemic and the proliferation of unverified remedies.

The alleged document, details of which remain unclear, has been shared widely on social media platforms in recent days, prompting concern among health officials. The MINSA released a statement reiterating that its official recommendations regarding COVID-19 prevention and treatment are only available through verified channels, including its official website and social media accounts. The ministry urged the public to be wary of unsubstantiated claims and to consult with healthcare professionals for accurate and reliable information.

The WHO echoed MINSA's statement, emphasizing its commitment to providing evidence-based guidelines for managing the pandemic. In a separate statement, the organization stressed that while some traditional remedies might offer symptomatic relief, there is no scientific evidence to support the claim that chewing ginger, or any other specific food, can prevent or cure COVID-19. The WHO continues to recommend preventative measures such as vaccination, mask-wearing, and social distancing to reduce the risk of infection.

The spread of misinformation surrounding COVID-19 has been a persistent challenge throughout the pandemic, leading to confusion and potentially harmful practices. Health organizations worldwide have been actively combating false claims by providing accurate information and debunking myths. Both the MINSA and the WHO encourage individuals to rely on trusted sources of information and to critically evaluate claims circulating online before sharing them. Consuming false remedies can be dangerous, and relying on them instead of proven medical treatments can have serious health consequences. The public is urged to verify information with official sources and healthcare professionals to stay informed and protect themselves from COVID-19.

article_summary: El Ministerio de Salud de Perú (MINSA) y la Organización Mundial de la Salud (OMS) han negado que recomienden chupar jengibre como medida preventiva o curativa contra el COVID-19, desmintiendo un documento difundido en redes sociales. Ambas instituciones advierten contra la desinformación y reiteraron que sus recomendaciones oficiales se encuentran en canales verificados, exhortando a la población a consultar a profesionales de la salud. La OMS destacó que no hay evidencia científica para afirmar que el jengibre prevenga o cure el virus, manteniendo su enfoque en vacunación, mascarillas y distanciamiento físico como medidas efectivas.
